criterion_notes.c1: Descriptively reports household water sources (including communal municipal taps, boreholes, rainwater, rivers, and springs), distance to water sources, and supply frequency in Section 3.3, alongside household water treatment and greywater recycling practices.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the study examines no legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism governing water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it also fails: the empirical survey maps household technological, agronomic, and indigenous knowledge WEF practices and perceived adoption drivers (knowledge, social networks, peers, reliability, environmental value, cost saving), while references to WEF sustainability governance, subsidized schemes, poor extension services, and proposed multi-stakeholder Innovation Platforms (IPs) appear only as unanalysed background commentary or normative policy recommendations rather than an empirically analysed governance factor affecting service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data from a mixed-methods cross-sectional study of 128 households across six villages in Vhembe District Municipality using semi-structured questionnaires, triangulated with key informant interviews (KIIs) and focus group discussions (FGDs).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports descriptive univariate water access indicators in Section 3.3 (use of communal municipal taps vs rainwater/river/borehole sources, distance within household vs within/beyond 1 km, and receiving municipal water less than three times a month or never), although the main outcomes analysed are awareness and uptake of WEF smart practices and technologies.
criterion_notes.c5: Population (128 households in six villages) and cross-sectional descriptive mixed-methods design are identifiable, but no legal, administrative, or governance exposure is empirically linked to any water or sanitation service access outcome; analysis is limited to univariate frequency tables of household practices and perceived technology-adoption factors.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 3 of 15 (Section 2.2 Scope of the study)
evidence_quotes.quote: The scope of the study involved identifying and quantifying the WEF nexus smart technologies, innovations, and practices in the study area.

Only those households who were available as scheduled (128 out of a possible 200) were interviewed. The information from household surveys was triangulated through key informant interviews (KII) and focus group discussions (FGDs).

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 6 of 15 (Section 3.3 Water resources access and use in the study area)
evidence_quotes.quote: About 29% of the respondents used communal municipal taps, with about 11% using boreholes (Table 6).

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 6 of 15 (Section 3.3 Water resources access and use in the study area)
evidence_quotes.quote: The majority (about 38%) of the households had access to water resources within the household, 34% within 1 km, and about 29% beyond 1 km of the household. However, the majority of the households either received water less than three times a month or never received it at all.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 11 of 15 (Section 3.12 Factors influencing water smart technologies)
evidence_quotes.quote: Only about 16% (20 in number) of the respondents were cognitive of the factors inﬂuencing smart water technologies. The reasons for the dismal cognition include lack of information, predominant subsidized water schemes as well as poor extension services.
The study has provided baseline data on existing smart WEF innovations and practices at the household level, Vhembe District Municipality.

raw_response.exposure: Cognitive, informational, social-network, and cost/reliability factors perceived to influence household adoption of WEF nexus smart technologies and indigenous knowledge practices (no legal, administrative, or governance exposure governing water service access examined)
raw_response.outcome: Household awareness and adoption of WEF smart innovations/practices (rainwater harvesting, boiling/chlorination, water recycling, solar energy, conservation agriculture, food preservation, indigenous knowledge), plus univariate descriptive baseline water sources, distance, and supply frequency
raw_response.population_and_sample: 128 households across six rural villages (Siloam, Phadzima, Khalavha, Sambandou, Malavuwe, and Tshakhuma) in the Nzhelele and Luvuvhu river catchments, Vhembe District Municipality, Limpopo Province, South Africa, supplemented by key informant interviews and focus group discussions
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although this empirical cross-sectional mixed-methods household study (n = 128 households) descriptively reports household water sources, distance to water, and low supply frequency in Vhembe District Municipality, South Africa, its scope and empirical analysis focus on mapping household water-energy-food (WEF) nexus technologies, agronomic/food preservation practices, and indigenous knowledge systems, along with cognitive, informational, and social-network perceptions of technology adoption. It does not empirically examine any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance mechanism governing water or sanitation service access (neither under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading nor under the plain wording of Criterion 2), nor does it link any governance exposure to a water or sanitation access outcome.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods descriptive study (semi-structured household survey with key informant interviews and focus group discussions)
